rv.q: A Few Good Men, even in a production as generously appointed and grandly performed as this, offers truths that just aren’t that hard to handle.
Arden’s production works as theater only intermittently.

That said, “A Few Good Men” is a bona fide audience pleaser, a craftful and engrossing piece of writing, even if this very expansive staging with four additional actors from what is typical (the gifted designer Dane Laffrey has re-created much of the Navy base, it feels) pushes it to its limit.
The production may not generate much excitement, but it earns a respectful salute—the proper response to a show whose duties have been discharged honorably, if not with special distinction.
Director Michael Arden’s ginormous revival has a few good sequences and a few good performances, but “A Few Good Men,” which opened Thursday night on Broadway, has never really been a good play.
While there’s plenty of high competency on display in A Few Good Men, the stalwart traditionalism at its core makes it a strange and unsettling choice for revivification.
Unfortunately both Ms. Rodriguez and Mr. Blyth give lusterless performances.
It’s a starchy, listless production that never finds a proper sense of scale.

It’s a tough act to follow, but under Arden’s crackling direction, “A Few Good Men” is as explosively compelling as ever in a bang-up revival that opened Oct. 29 at Lincoln Center’s Vivian Beaumont Theater.

As the sole female principal, Rodriguez drives the production. Her plucky Galloway is loaded with charisma and gumption — and a consistent refusal to accept “no” as an answer. She pokes and prods, unrelenting in her pursuit of the truth. Honestly, it’s exhausting to watch her jump through hoops and repeatedly justify her belonging in these rooms.
Michael Arden’s taut direction and Dane Laffrey’s superb use of the vast Beaumont stage prove to be the true stars here...

If “A Few Good Men” hasn’t exactly gained profundity, it still, in the hands of these performers, provides crackling entertainment — and raises questions that are at least as timely today as they were 37 years ago.
The British star proves he has the chops to be a real leading man as Lieutenant Daniel Kaffee, the cocky lawyer who hasn’t seen the inside of a courtroom — until now.
If you go to the current Lincoln Center Theater revival of Aaron Sorkin’s play expecting a replica of the high-octane Hollywood legal thriller, you’ll be disappointed.
In short, this is as it always was, a thinly plotted, old-school courtroom melodrama.
It’s an artifact rather than a masterwork, an impressive piece of juvenilia that is less sophisticated than the work Sorkin would go on to create less than a decade later.
It's less a revelatory revival than a probable case of misplaced affection.

Sorkin’s brand prominence is surely the truest explanation for why this play, although often portentous and glib, and long overshadowed by the later blockbuster movie version, is getting a monumentally staged, occasionally riveting, but ultimately unmemorable Broadway revival.

Yet for all the strengths of Lincoln Center Theater’s sleek new revival of Sorkin’s military drama, at the Vivian Beaumont through January 10, the biggest letdown is how leaden those same courtroom battles suddenly feel.
Aaron Sorkin's 1989 military courtroom drama receives an uneven Broadway revival.
A Few Good Men offers solid performances from the revival’s cast, with actors like John Zdrojeski inspiring true terror...
“A Few Good Men” is a creaky old play.

Director Michael Arden’s glossy Broadway revival is a gripping piece of storytelling, and the production boasts an almost cinematic grandeur that makes the most of the cavernous stage at Lincoln Center’s Vivian Beaumont Theater.

Director Michael Arden (The Lost Boys) handles Sorkin’s dense script with a deft hand, navigating a sprawling stage conceived by scenic designer Dane Laffrey as a military airstrip and 20 other locations, brought into focus by Japhy Weideman’s precise lighting.
The production may not generate much excitement, but it earns a respectful salute.

cn.t: Sorkin's military courtroom drama receives a handsomely staged but uneven revival that critics find workmanlike and overlong. While Arden's direction and the production values earn praise, most agree the play feels dated and can't escape its iconic film adaptation's shadow.

lo.t: Opens 12 AM day before performance, closes 3 PM day before. Winners drawn at 10 AM and 3 PM.

vs.sum: The Vivian Beaumont Theater offers exceptional sightlines and sound quality due to its unique thrust stage design, ensuring a great view and auditory experience from nearly every seat. While the ambiance is enhanced by its location within the Lincoln Center, the comfort level is average with some reports of tight seating, and facilities are typical for a Broadway venue.
